items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The minimum potential difference needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons reaching the collector, eVₛ = Eₖ,max"?
items.answer: stopping potential
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of stopping potential.

items.stem: Maya writes: "The stopping potential depends on the intensity of the light." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: eVₛ = hf − Φ depends only on frequency and work function.
items.markingKey: eVₛ = hf − Φ depends only on frequency and work function. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the wave model of light and the photon model of light.
items.answer: The wave model treats light energy as continuous and spread over the wavefront, depending on intensity; the photon model treats light as quanta of energy hf, each absorbed by a single electron, so frequency determines whether emission occurs.
items.markingKey: The wave model treats light energy as continuous and spread over the wavefront, depending on intensity; the photon model treats light as quanta of energy hf, each absorbed by a single electron, so frequency determines whether emission occurs. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Photons of energy 4.0 eV fall on magnesium (work function 3.7 eV). What is the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons?
The work function of platinum is 5.6 eV. Calculate its threshold frequency and the corresponding wavelength.
items.answer: f₀ = 1.35 × 10¹⁵ Hz; λ₀ = 222 nm

items.stem: Solar panels work by absorbing photons, not by the photoelectric effect itself. Compare the two processes, explaining why both show a threshold photon energy and why sunlight of longer wavelength cannot be used by either.
items.answer: In the photoelectric effect photons eject electrons from the metal surface (needs hf ≥ Φ, a few eV); in a solar cell photons raise electrons across the band gap (≈ 1.1 eV for silicon) to create current. Both need a minimum photon energy, set by Φ or the band gap; longer-wavelength photons have hf below this threshold.
items.markingKey: In the photoelectric effect photons eject electrons from the metal surface (needs hf ≥ Φ, a few eV); in a solar cell photons raise electrons across the band gap (≈ 1.1 eV for silicon) to create current. Both need a minimum photon energy, set by Φ or the band gap; longer-wavelength photons have hf below this threshold.

items.stem: "Einstein’s explanation of the photoelectric effect was accepted immediately." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: It was accepted only after precise experiments confirmed its predictions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it explained threshold frequency and Eₖ independent of intensity. Arguments against: many physicists, including Planck, resisted light quanta for years; Millikan set out to disprove it and confirmed it in 1916; acceptance required experimental tests (NOS). Supported judgement: It was accepted only after precise experiments confirmed its predictions. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Define the term "threshold frequency".
items.answer: The minimum frequency of radiation that causes photoelectric emission from a given metal, f₀ = Φ/h

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "stopping potential"?
options: The minimum potential difference needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons reaching the collector, eVₛ = Eₖ,max
The wavelength λ = h/p associated with a particle of momentum p
The idea that matter and radiation both show wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experiment
The quantity h/(mₑc) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m, the scale of the wavelength shift in Compton scattering
items.answer: The minimum potential difference needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons reaching the collector, eVₛ = Eₖ,max
items.markingKey: A. "stopping potential" is the minimum potential difference needed to stop the most energetic photoelectrons reaching the collector, eVₛ = Eₖ,max.

items.stem: Increasing the intensity of light above the threshold frequency
options: increases the number of photoelectrons emitted per second
items.answer: increases the number of photoelectrons emitted per second
items.markingKey: C. More photons per second, same photon energy.

items.stem: Which of the following statements about the photoelectric effect and the photon model is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Amara.)
options: Λ = h/(mv): doubling v halves λ.
Brighter light (more photons) increases the number of electrons emitted per second, not their maximum kinetic energy, which depends only on frequency.
The stopping potential depends on the intensity of the light.
All matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; diffraction has been observed for neutrons, atoms and even large molecules (C₆₀).
items.answer: The stopping potential depends on the intensity of the light.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: eVₛ = hf − Φ depends only on frequency and work function.

items.stem: Graphs of Eₖ,max against frequency for two different metals are
options: lines of different gradient through the origin
items.answer: parallel lines with different intercepts
items.markingKey: B. Gradient h for all; intercept −Φ differs.

items.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, predict and explain the effect on the photocurrent and the stopping potential when the intensity of the light is doubled at constant frequency.
items.answer: The photocurrent doubles but the stopping potential is unchanged: twice as many photons per second, each with the same energy hf.
items.markingKey: the photocurrent doubles but the stopping potential is unchanged (A1 A1); twice as many photons per second, each with the same energy hf (R1).

items.stem: Explain why photoemission is observed to be instantaneous, even at very low intensity.
items.answer: Energy is delivered in discrete photons; a single photon above threshold gives enough energy to one electron immediately, whereas the wave model predicts a delay while energy accumulates.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Energy is delivered in discrete photons; a single photon above threshold gives enough energy to one electron immediately, whereas the wave model predicts a delay while energy accumulates. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, predict and explain the effect on the photocurrent and the stopping potential when the frequency is increased at constant intensity (power).
items.answer: The stopping potential increases, but the photocurrent decreases slightly: each photon has more energy, but fewer photons arrive per second for the same power.
items.markingKey: the stopping potential increases, but the photocurrent decreases slightly (A1 A1); each photon has more energy, but fewer photons arrive per second for the same power (R1).

items.stem: "If the frequency is doubled, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons doubles." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Eₖ,max = hf − Φ: doubling f more than doubles Eₖ,max because Φ is subtracted.

items.markingKey: hc/λ = 3.11 eV (M1); eVₛ = hf − Φ (M1); Vₛ = 1.01 V (A1).

Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The photoelectric effect proves that light is made of particles."
items.answer: It is strong evidence for the photon (quantum) model of energy exchange, but light is best described by wave–particle duality.

Arguments against: interference and diffraction need a wave description; light shows wave–particle duality; experiments support models rather than prove them (NOS). items.answer: It was accepted only after precise experiments confirmed its predictions.

items.stem: In a photoelectric experiment on an unknown metal, the stopping potential is 0.801 V for light of frequency 7.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz and 1.63 V for 9.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz. (a) Determine a value for the Planck constant. (b) Determine the work function of the metal in eV and suggest its identity. (c) Sketch the graph of Vₛ against f and state the significance of its intercepts. (d) Explain why a graph of photocurrent against intensity at constant frequency is a straight line through the origin.
items.answer: (a) h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; (b) Φ = 2.1 eV (caesium); (c) f-intercept = threshold frequency 5.07 × 10¹⁴ Hz, V-intercept = −Φ/e; (d) number of photons ∝ intensity, each releasing at most one electron
items.markingKey: (a) gradient = ΔVₛ/Δf = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s (M1); h = e × gradient = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (A1). (b) Φ = hf₁ − eV₁ = 2.1 eV (M1 A1). (c) intercepts identified (R1). (d) photon model (R1).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The diffraction of an electron beam by the regular array of atoms in a crystal, demonstrating the wave nature of electrons"?
items.answer: electron diffraction
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of electron diffraction.

items.stem: Electron diffraction is evidence that
items.answer: electrons have wave properties
items.markingKey: B. Diffraction is a wave phenomenon.

items.stem: A student claims: "Only electrons have a de Broglie wavelength." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: All matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; diffraction has been observed for neutrons, atoms and even large molecules (C₆₀).
items.markingKey: All matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; diffraction has been observed for neutrons, atoms and even large molecules (C₆₀). 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of a dust grain of mass 1.00 × 10⁻¹² kg moving at 0.010 m s⁻¹, and comment on whether its wave nature could be observed.
items.answer: 6.63 × 10⁻²⁰ m; far too small to observe
items.markingKey: λ = h/(mv) (M1) = 6.63 × 10⁻²⁰ m (A1); much smaller than any aperture or atom, so no observable diffraction (R1).

items.stem: What momentum must a particle have for its de Broglie wavelength to be 3.88 × 10⁻¹¹ m?
items.answer: 1.71 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. p = h/λ = 1.71 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹.

items.stem: In an electron-diffraction tube, electrons accelerated through 4.0 kV pass through a graphite film and produce rings on a screen 0.14 m away. (a) Calculate the de Broglie wavelength. (b) The inner ring has radius 11 mm; using sin θ ≈ r/(2L) for the Bragg geometry, estimate the atomic spacing. (c) Predict and explain the change in ring size at 6.0 kV. (d) Explain how this experiment supports de Broglie’s hypothesis.
items.answer: (a) λ = h/√(2meV) = 1.94 × 10⁻¹¹ m; (b) θ ≈ 0.011/0.28 = 0.0393 rad, d = λ/(2 sin θ) ≈ 2.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; (c) λ ∝ 1/√V, so the rings shrink by a factor √(4/6) = 0.82 (radius ≈ 9.0 mm); (d) the rings are a diffraction pattern whose size changes with V exactly as λ = h/p predicts.
items.markingKey: λ (M1 A1); spacing estimate (M1 A1); prediction with factor (R1); link between observed scaling and λ = h/p (R1).

items.stem: Electrons accelerated through a larger potential difference have
items.answer: a shorter de Broglie wavelength
items.markingKey: B. More momentum.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "de Broglie wavelength".
items.answer: The wavelength λ = h/p associated with a particle of momentum p
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the wavelength λ = h/p associated with a particle of momentum p. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: A teacher in Seoul asks a class to choose the one correct statement about matter waves and the de Broglie wavelength. Which statement should be chosen?
options: The stopping potential depends on the intensity of the light.
Doubling the speed of an electron doubles its de Broglie wavelength.
All matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; diffraction has been observed for neutrons, atoms and even large molecules (C₆₀).
items.answer: All matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; diffraction has been observed for neutrons, atoms and even large molecules (C₆₀).
items.markingKey: D. The other options are common misconceptions. All matter has a de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p; diffraction has been observed for neutrons, atoms and even large molecules (C₆₀).

items.stem: Predict and explain what happens to the de Broglie wavelength and the observed diffraction when an electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy.
items.answer: The electron has the longer wavelength, because p = √(2mEₖ) is smaller for the smaller mass.
items.markingKey: the electron has the longer wavelength (A1); p = √(2mEₖ) is smaller for the smaller mass (R1).

items.stem: Distinguish between the de Broglie wavelength of an electron and the wavelength of a photon of the same energy.
items.answer: For an electron λ = h/√(2mEₖ); for a photon λ = hc/E. For the same (non-relativistic) energy the electron’s wavelength is much shorter because its momentum is much larger.
items.markingKey: For an electron λ = h/√(2mEₖ); for a photon λ = hc/E. For the same (non-relativistic) energy the electron’s wavelength is much shorter because its momentum is much larger. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why electron microscopes can resolve much finer detail than optical microscopes.
items.answer: Electrons accelerated through kilovolts have de Broglie wavelengths of ~10⁻¹¹ m, far smaller than visible light (~5 × 10⁻⁷ m); resolution is limited by diffraction, which is smaller for shorter wavelengths.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Electrons accelerated through kilovolts have de Broglie wavelengths of ~10⁻¹¹ m, far smaller than visible light (~5 × 10⁻⁷ m); resolution is limited by diffraction, which is smaller for shorter wavelengths. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.markingKey: D. p = h/λ = 1.21 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹.

items.answer: λ = h/(mv): doubling v halves λ.

items.stem: "De Broglie’s hypothesis was accepted because it was mathematically elegant." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Elegance made the idea attractive, but acceptance came from experimental confirmation of electron diffraction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it linked Bohr’s quantisation to standing waves; symmetry between light and matter was appealing. Arguments against: acceptance followed experimental confirmation by Davisson–Germer and G. P. Thomson (1927); elegance alone is not sufficient evidence (NOS). Supported judgement: Elegance made the idea attractive, but acceptance came from experimental confirmation of electron diffraction. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: (a) Davisson and Germer directed 100 eV electrons at a nickel crystal whose surface atoms are 2.15 × 10⁻¹⁰ m apart. Calculate the de Broglie wavelength of the electrons and the angle of the first-order maximum given by d sin θ = λ. (b) An electron microscope uses electrons accelerated through 10.0 kV. Calculate their (non-relativistic) wavelength and compare it with visible light. (c) Explain why the non-relativistic formula becomes inaccurate at the highest voltages.
items.answer: (a) 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m, 34.8°; (b) 1.23 × 10⁻¹¹ m, about 4.1 × 10⁴ times shorter than 500 nm light; (c) electron speeds approach c, so p ≠ √(2meV)
items.markingKey: (a) λ = h/√(2meV) (M1) = 1.23 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (A1); θ = sin⁻¹(λ/d) = 34.8° (A1). (b) λ = 1.23 × 10⁻¹¹ m (A1); comparison (A1). (c) relativistic momentum needed as v → c (R1).

items.stem: A transmission electron microscope in Tokyo accelerates electrons through 20 kV. (a) Calculate the non-relativistic de Broglie wavelength of the electrons. (b) Compare the result with the shortest wavelength of visible light (400 nm) and explain why electron microscopes resolve much finer detail. (c) The engineers double the accelerating voltage. Determine the factor by which the wavelength changes. (d) Discuss whether the non-relativistic formula remains reliable at this voltage.
items.answer: (a) λ = 8.68 × 10⁻¹² m; (b) about 4.6 × 10⁴ times shorter, and resolution scales with wavelength; (c) λ ∝ V^(−1/2), so λ falls by 1/√2 = 0.707; (d) the kinetic energy is a noticeable fraction of mₑc² = 511 keV, so relativistic corrections of a few per cent or more are needed.
items.markingKey: (a) p = √(2meV) (M1), λ = h/p = 8.68 × 10⁻¹² m (A1). (b) ratio (A1) + resolution argument (R1). (c) factor 0.707 (A1). (d) compares eV with 511 keV (R1).

options: a longer wavelength than the incident photon
items.answer: a longer wavelength than the incident photon
items.markingKey: D. It transfers energy to the electron.

items.answer: about 1800 times smaller

items.answer: 3.31 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: A. p = h/λ = 3.31 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹.

items.stem: A student claims: "In Compton scattering, the photon slows down." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases.
items.markingKey: Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Gamma photons of 662 keV from caesium-137 are detected after Compton scattering in a detector. (a) Show that the maximum energy that can be transferred to an electron (the "Compton edge") is about 478 keV. (b) Explain why the detector records a continuous range of electron energies below this. (c) Explain why the photopeak at 662 keV also appears.
items.answer: (a) back-scatter: λ′ = λ + 2h/mₑc; E′ = 184 keV, so Eₖ,max = 662 − 184 = 478 keV; (b) scattering angles from 0° to 180° give all energies from 0 to 478 keV; (c) some photons are fully absorbed (photoelectric absorption or multiple scatters), depositing all 662 keV.
items.markingKey: (a) back-scatter: λ′ = λ + 2h/mₑc; E′ = 184 keV, so Eₖ,max = 662 − 184 = 478 keV; (b) scattering angles from 0° to 180° give all energies from 0 to 478 keV; (c) some photons are fully absorbed (photoelectric absorption or multiple scatters), depositing all 662 keV.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "Compton scattering".
items.answer: The scattering of an X-ray or gamma-ray photon by a free electron, in which the photon loses energy and its wavelength increases
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the scattering of an X-ray or gamma-ray photon by a free electron, in which the photon loses energy and its wavelength increases. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Mohammed writes four statements while revising Compton scattering. Which one is a misconception?
options: Eₖ,max = hf − Φ: doubling f more than doubles Eₖ,max because Φ is subtracted.
Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) depends only on angle; the fractional shift Δλ/λ is larger for higher-energy photons.
In Compton scattering, the photon slows down.
Λ = h/(mv): doubling v halves λ.
items.answer: In Compton scattering, the photon slows down.
items.markingKey: C. This is incorrect: Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the photoelectric effect and Compton scattering.
items.answer: In the photoelectric effect a photon is completely absorbed and its energy frees a bound electron; in Compton scattering the photon is scattered by an essentially free electron, losing only part of its energy and continuing with a longer wavelength.
items.markingKey: In the photoelectric effect a photon is completely absorbed and its energy frees a bound electron; in Compton scattering the photon is scattered by an essentially free electron, losing only part of its energy and continuing with a longer wavelength. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why the Compton effect could not be explained by the classical wave model.
items.answer: Classically, an electromagnetic wave would make electrons oscillate at the incident frequency and re-radiate at the same frequency; the observed angle-dependent increase in wavelength requires a particle-like collision with photon momentum h/λ.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Classically, an electromagnetic wave would make electrons oscillate at the incident frequency and re-radiate at the same frequency; the observed angle-dependent increase in wavelength requires a particle-like collision with photon momentum h/λ. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: In an investigation the relationship Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) for X-rays scattered at different angles is expected. Explain how a linear graph can be used to verify this relationship and to determine a value from the gradient.
items.answer: Plot Δλ (y-axis) against (1 − cos θ) (x-axis); gradient = h/(mₑc), the Compton wavelength. A straight line through the origin confirms the Compton formula.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: Δλ against (1 − cos θ) (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = h/(mₑc), the Compton wavelength (A1). A straight line through the origin confirms the Compton formula.

items.stem: Calculate the momentum of an X-ray photon of wavelength 7.10 × 10⁻¹² m and its energy in keV.
items.answer: p = 9.34 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹; E = 175 keV
items.markingKey: p = h/λ (M1) = 9.34 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ (A1); E = pc = 175 keV (A1).

items.stem: What is the Compton shift for photons scattered by free electrons through 60°?
A photon of wavelength 5.00 × 10⁻¹² m is Compton-scattered by a free electron through 180°. By how much does its wavelength increase?
items.markingKey: D. Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos 180°) = 4.85 × 10⁻¹² m, independent of λ.

items.stem: In a Compton experiment, 20 keV photons scattered at 60° are detected. (a) Determine the energy of the scattered photons. (b) Calculate the momenta of the incident and scattered photons. (c) Explain how conservation of momentum determines the direction of the recoiling electron. (d) Suggest why the effect was first observed with X-rays rather than visible light.
items.answer: (a) 19.6 keV; (b) 1.07 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ and 1.05 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹; (c) electron momentum = vector difference of photon momenta; (d) Δλ ≈ pm, negligible compared with visible wavelengths
items.markingKey: (a) λ = 6.22 × 10⁻¹¹ m, λ′ = 6.34 × 10⁻¹¹ m (M1), E′ = 19.6 keV (A1). (b) p = h/λ (M1) values (A1). (c) vector diagram: p_e = p − p′ (R1). (d) fractional shift argument (R1).

items.stem: Discuss how Compton scattering and the photoelectric effect together support the photon model of electromagnetic radiation, explaining what each experiment shows about photon energy and photon momentum.
items.answer: The photoelectric effect shows that energy is absorbed in quanta E = hf (threshold frequency, Eₖ independent of intensity, instant emission). Compton scattering shows photons also carry momentum p = h/λ: the angle-dependent wavelength shift Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) follows exactly from conserving energy and momentum in a photon–electron collision. Together they show light interacts as particles with both energy and momentum, while interference still requires wave behaviour.
items.markingKey: Photoelectric evidence for E = hf (R1 R1); Compton evidence for p = h/λ (R1 R1); conservation laws used (R1); duality comment (A1).

items.stem: The gradient of a graph of maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons against frequency is
items.answer: the Planck constant h
items.markingKey: A. Eₖ,max = hf − Φ.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "wave–particle duality"?
options: The idea that matter and radiation both show wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experiment
The scattering of an X-ray or gamma-ray photon by a free electron, in which the photon loses energy and its wavelength increases
The wavelength λ = h/p associated with a particle of momentum p
The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal, Φ
items.answer: The idea that matter and radiation both show wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experiment
items.markingKey: A. "wave–particle duality" is the idea that matter and radiation both show wave-like and particle-like properties depending on the experiment.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Compton scattering"?
options: The minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface of a metal, Φ
The scattering of an X-ray or gamma-ray photon by a free electron, in which the photon loses energy and its wavelength increases
The quantity h/(mₑc) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m, the scale of the wavelength shift in Compton scattering
The emission of electrons from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation above a certain frequency falls on it
items.answer: The scattering of an X-ray or gamma-ray photon by a free electron, in which the photon loses energy and its wavelength increases
items.markingKey: B. "Compton scattering" is the scattering of an X-ray or gamma-ray photon by a free electron, in which the photon loses energy and its wavelength increases.

items.stem: Ingrid writes four statements while revising the photoelectric effect and the photon model. Which one is a misconception?
options: The stopping potential depends on the intensity of the light.
Λ = h/(mv): doubling v halves λ.
Brighter light (more photons) increases the number of electrons emitted per second, not their maximum kinetic energy, which depends only on frequency.
Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) depends only on angle; the fractional shift Δλ/λ is larger for higher-energy photons.
items.answer: The stopping potential depends on the intensity of the light.
items.markingKey: A. This is incorrect: eVₛ = hf − Φ depends only on frequency and work function.

items.stem: Predict and explain what happens to the de Broglie wavelength and the observed diffraction when the accelerating voltage of an electron beam is quadrupled.
items.answer: The de Broglie wavelength halves and the diffraction rings shrink, because p ∝ √V, so λ = h/p ∝ 1/√V.
items.markingKey: the de Broglie wavelength halves and the diffraction rings shrink (A1); p ∝ √V, so λ = h/p ∝ 1/√V (R1).

items.stem: Explain the difference between Compton scattering and the photoelectric effect.
items.answer: In the photoelectric effect a photon is completely absorbed and its energy frees a bound electron; in Compton scattering the photon is scattered by an essentially free electron, losing only part of its energy and continuing with a longer wavelength.
items.markingKey: In the photoelectric effect a photon is completely absorbed and its energy frees a bound electron; in Compton scattering the photon is scattered by an essentially free electron, losing only part of its energy and continuing with a longer wavelength. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the photon model of light and the wave model of light.
items.answer: The wave model treats light energy as continuous and spread over the wavefront, depending on intensity; the photon model treats light as quanta of energy hf, each absorbed by a single electron, so frequency determines whether emission occurs.
items.markingKey: The wave model treats light energy as continuous and spread over the wavefront, depending on intensity; the photon model treats light as quanta of energy hf, each absorbed by a single electron, so frequency determines whether emission occurs. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Which of the following statements about matter waves and the de Broglie wavelength is a common misconception? (Revision quiz set by Leila.)
options: Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases.
Brighter light (more photons) increases the number of electrons emitted per second, not their maximum kinetic energy, which depends only on frequency.
Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) depends only on angle; the fractional shift Δλ/λ is larger for higher-energy photons.
Doubling the speed of an electron doubles its de Broglie wavelength.
items.answer: Doubling the speed of an electron doubles its de Broglie wavelength.
items.markingKey: D. This is incorrect: λ = h/(mv): doubling v halves λ.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "The Compton shift increases with the energy of the incident photon." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) depends only on angle; the fractional shift Δλ/λ is larger for higher-energy photons.
items.markingKey: Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) depends only on angle; the fractional shift Δλ/λ is larger for higher-energy photons. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: The work function of calcium is 2.9 eV. Calculate its threshold frequency and the corresponding wavelength.
items.answer: f₀ = 7.00 × 10¹⁴ Hz; λ₀ = 429 nm

items.stem: An electron is accelerated from rest through 1000 V. What is its de Broglie wavelength?
Calculate the momentum of an X-ray photon of wavelength 1.00 × 10⁻¹¹ m and its energy in keV.
items.answer: p = 6.63 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹; E = 124 keV
items.markingKey: p = h/λ (M1) = 6.63 × 10⁻²³ kg m s⁻¹ (A1); E = pc = 124 keV (A1).

items.answer: 138 keV

items.stem: Chloé writes: "Brighter light makes photoelectrons faster." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Brighter light (more photons) increases the number of electrons emitted per second, not their maximum kinetic energy, which depends only on frequency.
items.markingKey: Brighter light (more photons) increases the number of electrons emitted per second, not their maximum kinetic energy, which depends only on frequency. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Neutrons from a reactor are slowed to 2.2 km s⁻¹ and diffracted by a crystal. (a) Calculate their de Broglie wavelength. (b) Explain why neutrons, rather than X-rays, are used to locate hydrogen atoms in crystals. (c) Explain why electrons of the same wavelength would not penetrate the crystal as far.
items.answer: (a) λ = h/(mv) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2200) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; (b) X-rays scatter from electrons, and hydrogen has only one; neutrons scatter from nuclei; (c) electrons are charged and interact strongly with atoms via electric forces, so they are absorbed near the surface.
items.markingKey: (a) λ = h/(mv) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(1.675 × 10⁻²⁷ × 2200) = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; (b) X-rays scatter from electrons, and hydrogen has only one; neutrons scatter from nuclei; (c) electrons are charged and interact strongly with atoms via electric forces, so they are absorbed near the surface.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Photons have momentum but no mass, so the idea of photon momentum is contradictory."
items.answer: Not contradictory: the Newtonian definition is a special case; relativity and experiment show light carries momentum p = h/λ.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: in Newtonian mechanics p = mv requires mass. Arguments against: relativity gives E² = (pc)² + (mc²)², so massless particles have p = E/c; Compton scattering and radiation pressure (solar sails) confirm photon momentum. Supported judgement: Not contradictory: the Newtonian definition is a special case; relativity and experiment show light carries momentum p = h/λ. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "Einstein’s explanation of the photoelectric effect was accepted immediately." Discuss.
items.answer: It was accepted only after precise experiments confirmed its predictions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it explained threshold frequency and Eₖ independent of intensity. Arguments against: many physicists, including Planck, resisted light quanta for years; Millikan set out to disprove it and confirmed it in 1916; acceptance required experimental tests (NOS). Supported judgement: It was accepted only after precise experiments confirmed its predictions. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: "Wave–particle duality means electrons are sometimes waves and sometimes particles." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Electrons are neither classical waves nor particles; both models are partial descriptions of quantum behaviour (NOS: models and their limits).
items.markingKey: Arguments for: some experiments show interference (wave), others localised detection (particle). Arguments against: electrons are quantum objects described by wavefunctions; "wave" and "particle" are classical models; complementarity: each experiment reveals one aspect. Supported judgement: Electrons are neither classical waves nor particles; both models are partial descriptions of quantum behaviour (NOS: models and their limits). Markbands (15 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The minimum frequency of radiation that causes photoelectric emission from a given metal, f₀ = Φ/h"?
items.answer: threshold frequency
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of threshold frequency.

items.stem: Which experiment first confirmed the wave nature of electrons?
options: Davisson and Germer’s scattering of electrons from a nickel crystal
items.answer: Davisson and Germer’s scattering of electrons from a nickel crystal
items.markingKey: C. 1927 diffraction maxima matched λ = h/p.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The quantity h/(mₑc) = 2.43 × 10⁻¹² m, the scale of the wavelength shift in Compton scattering"?
items.answer: Compton wavelength
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of Compton wavelength.

items.stem: Explain why the wave model of light cannot explain the existence of a threshold frequency.
items.answer: In the wave model energy arrives continuously and depends on intensity, so any frequency should eventually liberate electrons if the light is intense enough or shines long enough; the observation that no electrons are emitted below f₀ regardless of intensity contradicts this.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: In the wave model energy arrives continuously and depends on intensity, so any frequency should eventually liberate electrons if the light is intense enough or shines long enough; the observation that no electrons are emitted below f₀ regardless of intensity contradicts this. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the wavelength of a photon of the same energy and the de Broglie wavelength of an electron.
items.answer: For an electron λ = h/√(2mEₖ); for a photon λ = hc/E. For the same (non-relativistic) energy the electron’s wavelength is much shorter because its momentum is much larger.
items.markingKey: For an electron λ = h/√(2mEₖ); for a photon λ = hc/E. For the same (non-relativistic) energy the electron’s wavelength is much shorter because its momentum is much larger. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Maya and a classmate in Singapore disagree about Compton scattering. Which statement is correct?
options: The Compton shift increases with the energy of the incident photon.
Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases.
The stopping potential depends on the intensity of the light.
items.answer: Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases.
items.markingKey: B. The other options are common misconceptions. Photons always travel at c; the photon’s energy and frequency decrease, so its wavelength increases.

items.stem: In a photoelectric experiment, predict and explain the effect on the photocurrent and the stopping potential when the metal is replaced by one with a larger work function.
items.answer: The stopping potential decreases and the threshold frequency increases: more energy is needed to release each electron, so Eₖ,max = hf − Φ falls.
items.markingKey: the stopping potential decreases and the threshold frequency increases (A1 A1); more energy is needed to release each electron, so Eₖ,max = hf − Φ falls (R1).

items.stem: A proton and an electron have the same kinetic energy. Which has the longer de Broglie wavelength?
items.answer: the electron
items.markingKey: C. p = √(2mEₖ) is smaller for the electron.

items.stem: Outline how the data from an experiment testing Δλ = (h/mₑc)(1 − cos θ) for X-rays scattered at different angles should be linearised, and state the features of the graph that would confirm the relationship.
items.answer: Plot Δλ (y-axis) against (1 − cos θ) (x-axis); gradient = h/(mₑc), the Compton wavelength. A straight line through the origin confirms the Compton formula.
items.markingKey: Correct choice of axes: Δλ against (1 − cos θ) (M1); straight line expected (R1); gradient = h/(mₑc), the Compton wavelength (A1). A straight line through the origin confirms the Compton formula.

items.stem: "Brighter light makes photoelectrons faster." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Brighter light (more photons) increases the number of electrons emitted per second, not their maximum kinetic energy, which depends only on frequency.

items.answer: 8.54 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹

items.stem:
Light from a mercury lamp with filters illuminates a photocell with a caesium cathode. The stopping potential Vₛ is measured for each frequency f. Theory: eVₛ = hf − Φ.

f / 10¹⁴ Hz | Vₛ / V
8.22 | 1.29
7.41 | 0.97
6.88 | 0.75
6.10 | 0.44
5.49 | 0.17

(a) State the quantities that should be plotted to obtain a straight line. [1]
(b) Using the data, determine the gradient of the best-fit line. [2]
(c) Hence determine the Planck constant. [1]
(d) The gradients of the maximum and minimum lines differ from the best-fit gradient by ±3 %. State h with its absolute uncertainty. [1]
items.answer: (a) Vₛ (y) against f in Hz (x); (b) gradient ≈ 4.09 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s; (c) 6.55 × 10⁻³⁴ J s; (d) 6.55 × 10⁻³⁴ J s ± 2 × 10⁻³⁵ J s
items.markingKey: (a) Vₛ (y) against f in Hz (x) (A1). (b) Best-fit line through the plotted points (M1); gradient ≈ 4.09 × 10⁻¹⁵ V s – accept ±3 % (A1). (c) h = e × gradient = 6.55 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (A1). (d) absolute uncertainty = 3 % of the value = 2 × 10⁻³⁵ J s; value quoted to the same precision (A1).

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "De Broglie’s hypothesis was accepted because it was mathematically elegant."
items.answer: Elegance made the idea attractive, but acceptance came from experimental confirmation of electron diffraction.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it linked Bohr’s quantisation to standing waves; symmetry between light and matter was appealing. Arguments against: acceptance followed experimental confirmation by Davisson–Germer and G. P. Thomson (1927); elegance alone is not sufficient evidence (NOS). Supported judgement: Elegance made the idea attractive, but acceptance came from experimental confirmation of electron diffraction.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "The photoelectric effect proves that light is made of particles."
items.answer: It is strong evidence for the photon (quantum) model of energy exchange, but light is best described by wave–particle duality.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: threshold frequency, instantaneous emission and Eₖ independent of intensity are explained by photons. Arguments against: interference and diffraction need a wave description; light shows wave–particle duality; experiments support models rather than prove them (NOS). Supported judgement: It is strong evidence for the photon (quantum) model of energy exchange, but light is best described by wave–particle duality. Markbands (10 marks): Top band: focused, balanced argument, well-chosen specific evidence, and a reasoned judgement that follows from the analysis.

items.stem: At the Institut Laue–Langevin in Grenoble, neutrons from a reactor are slowed in a moderator at 320 K and used to study crystal structures. (a) Estimate the mean kinetic energy of a thermal neutron, using E = (3/2)k_B T. (b) Hence determine its de Broglie wavelength. (c) Explain why thermal neutrons, rather than visible light, are suitable for probing atomic spacings of about 10⁻¹⁰ m. (d) Suggest one advantage neutrons have over X-rays for locating hydrogen atoms.
items.answer: (a) 6.62 × 10⁻²¹ J; (b) λ = 1.41 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; (c) λ is comparable with atomic spacing, so measurable diffraction occurs (visible light ≈ 5 × 10⁻⁷ m is far too long); (d) neutrons scatter from nuclei, so light atoms such as hydrogen scatter strongly, whereas X-rays scatter from electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) E = 1.5 × 1.38 × 10⁻²³ × 320 (M1) = 6.62 × 10⁻²¹ J (A1). (b) λ = h/√(2mE) (M1) = 1.41 × 10⁻¹⁰ m (A1). (c) λ ≈ atomic spacing → diffraction (R1). (d) nuclear scattering / independent of electron number (R1).
